Background: Consuming collagen hydrolysate (CH) may improve symptoms of exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD); however, its acute effects have not been compared to dairy protein (DP), the most commonly consumed form of protein supplement. Therefore, this study compared the effects of CH and DP on recovery from EIMD. Methods: Thirty-three males consumed either CH ( n = 11) or DP ( n = 11), containing 25 g of protein, or an isoenergetic placebo ( n = 11) immediately post-exercise and once daily for three days. Indices of EIMD were measured before and 30 min and 24, 48, and 72 h after 30 min of downhill running on a −15% slope at 80% of VO 2max speed. Results: Downhill running induced significant EIMD, with time effects (all p < 0.001) for the delayed onset of muscle soreness (visual analogue scale), countermovement jump height, isometric midthigh pull force, maximal voluntary isometric contraction force, running economy, and biomarkers of muscle damage (creatine kinase) and inflammation (interleukin-6, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein). However, no group or interaction effects (all p > 0.05) were observed for any of the outcome measures. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the post-exercise consumption of CH or DP does not improve indices of EIMD during the acute recovery period in recreationally active males. collagen hydrolysate delayed-onset muscle soreness exercise-induced muscle damage post-exercise recovery milk proteins Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, New Zealand HVN1943 This research was funded by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, New Zealand, grant number HVN1943. 1. Introduction Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) is caused by exercise that is strenuous, repetitive, novel, and/or involves eccentric muscle contractions, such as downhill running [ 1 ]. Whilst EIMD is temporary, and may be beneficial for future muscle adaptation [ 2 ], it can create problems for regular exercisers by impairing performance during subsequent bouts of exercise [ 3 ] and/or by causing a disruption to normal daily activities that are not otherwise an issue [ 4 ]. Therefore, timely recovery from EIMD is important. Nutritional supplements and functional foods may provide benefits for physical health [ 5 ], performance [ 6 ], and recovery from exercise [ 7 ]; however, although significant effort has been made to find nutritional interventions that alleviate the symptoms of EIMD, including omega-3 fatty acids, various amino acids, polyphenols, and herbal extracts, there is no strong consensus on the best option [ 8 ]. One intervention at the forefront of most recommendations is dairy protein (DP) [ 9 ], which includes whey, casein, and whole milk. The consumption of DP following EIMD is believed to improve recovery through the delivery of essential amino acids that enhance rates of muscle protein synthesis, thus promoting muscle repair [ 10 ]; however, this mechanism has been disputed [ 11 ]. Irrespective of the mechanism, whether consuming DP is beneficial for recovery remains unclear, with some studies showing that DP can alter markers of EIMD, including muscle function (for example, Brown et al. [ 12 ]; Buckley et al. [ 13 ]; Cooke et al. [ 14 ]), while others, including Gee et al. [ 15 ]; Nieman et al. [ 16 ]; Ormsbee et al. [ 17 ]; and Saracino et al. [ 18 ], have failed to see an effect. Moreover, the majority of research has shown that supplementing with protein, including DP, does not specifically reduce exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) [ 19 ]. Despite mixed evidence for its effects on EIMD, and a significant environmental footprint [ 20 ], DP’s convenience and effects on muscle protein synthesis make it the major contributor to a protein supplement industry that is expected to be worth over USD 10 billion by 2030 in the US alone [ 21 ]. In order to improve sustainability, reduce environmental harm, and open up new commercial markets, researchers (and the supplement industry) are increasingly interested in novel protein sources [ 22 ] and how they may impact recovery and performance [ 19 , 21 ]. Sourced from the underutilised by-products of the meat industry, bovine collagen is high in the non-essential amino acids used to synthesise collagen and remodel the extra-cellular matrix (ECM) [ 23 ]. Once ingested, collagen hydrolysates (CHs) are digested in the gastrointestinal tract to yield free amino acids [ 24 ], as well as collagen-specific di- and tripeptides, including hydroxyprolylglycine (Hyp-Gly) and prolylhydroxyproline (Pro-Hyp) [ 25 ]. These are absorbed intact, via specific transporters on the enterocyte brush border membranes [ 26 ], and are increased in circulation following the ingestion of CH [ 25 ]. Additionally, Pro-Hyp is produced naturally as a product of collagen degradation in damaged tissues [ 27 ], where it stimulates the proliferation of fibroblasts and subsequent collagen synthesis; collagen-derived Pro-Hyp is therefore considered a fibroblast growth-initiating factor [ 28 ]. The effect of endogenous, wound-derived Pro-Hyp appears to be enhanced by Pro-Hyp from dietary CH [ 27 ]; therefore, CHs may offer a simple and inexpensive approach to optimising recovery from connective tissue damage, as occurs with EIMD [ 2 ]. Damage to the ECM negatively impacts force transmission [ 29 ], storage and utilisation of elastic energy during the stretch-shortening cycle [ 30 ], and, because of the high density of nociceptors located in the ECM, may be a major contributor to DOMS [ 31 ]. As such, enhancing the rate of repair is likely important for recovery. Indeed, there is some, limited, evidence showing that CH attenuates several markers of EIMD, most notably DOMS [ 32 , 33 ] and movements that rely on the stretch-shortening cycle [ 30 , 32 ]. Greater evidence for such benefits may provide economic opportunities and optimise the use of a food industry waste product, thus helping to improve the sustainability and environmental impact of the protein industry by reducing the reliance on DP. Although studies have compared the effects of CH and DP on rates of protein synthesis [ 34 ], and a combination of whey and CH on EIMD [ 9 ], to date, the separate effects of DP and CH have not been directly compared. A greater understanding of whether either protein source is better than the other, or indeed better than a placebo, may help inform consumers who are considering protein supplementation as an aid for muscle recovery. Therefore, we compared the effects of CH and DP on acute recovery from EIMD. It was hypothesised that, when consumed in the days after eccentric exercise, CH would reduce ratings of DOMS, increase the recovery of muscle function, and attenuate bloodborne biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation following EIMD, to an equal or greater extent than an equivalent amount of protein from DP, and that both protein sources would be more effective than an isoenergetic placebo (PLA).

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Recovery from Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage (EIMD) induced by eccentric exercise (downhill running), and the effects of acute, post-exercise protein supplementation (collagen hydrolysate or dairy protein) on this recovery.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Dairy Protein (DP) is proposed to improve recovery by delivering essential amino acids to enhance muscle protein synthesis and repair, although this mechanism is disputed. Milk protein concentrate, containing whey and casein, may offer synergistic immediate and sustained effects. Collagen Hydrolysate (CH) is digested into free amino acids and specific di- and tripeptides (e.g., Hyp-Gly, Pro-Hyp). Pro-Hyp is absorbed intact and stimulates fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, acting as a fibroblast growth-initiating factor, enhancing endogenous wound-derived Pro-Hyp for connective tissue and ECM repair. Both protein sources are thought to have anti-inflammatory actions, and CH may aid ECM repair via non-essential amino acids and Pro-Hyp, potentially increasing intramuscular collagen or cellular repair through HIF- cp1, heat shock proteins, and other collagen synthetic pathway initiators. Carbohydrate can further enhance protein effects by promoting amino acid uptake, glycogen replenishment, energy for recovery, and improved net protein balance. However, acute post-exercise protein supplementation was found not to effectively expedite muscle recovery from eccentric exercise.
related_biomarkers: maximal voluntary isometric contractions (MVIC) peak force

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compared 25g of protein from Collagen Hydrolysate (CH) or Dairy Protein (DP) to an isoenergetic (1000 kJ), flavour-matched placebo. Both CH and DP supplements contained 25g of protein. When consumed immediately post-exercise and once daily for three days, neither CH nor DP showed significant group or interaction effects (all p > 0.05) on various indices of EIMD, including muscle soreness (p=0.063-0.065), muscle function (CMJ: p=0.332, IMTP: p=0.574, MVIC: p=0.559, running economy: p=0.153), or blood-borne markers (hsCRP: p=0.318, CK: p=0.488, IL-6: p=0.226) compared to the placebo. This acute post-exercise three-day supplementation period was potentially insufficient for benefit, suggesting that a prolonged period, possibly at least nine days of CH consumption prior to exercise, might be required for protective effects. Future research should explore different doses and combinations of proteins.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The findings are specific to the acute recovery period from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) in recreationally active males, induced by a single 30-minute bout of downhill running on a -15% slope at 80% of VO2max speed, a protocol known to specifically alter the measured indices. The study highlights that acute, post-exercise protein supplementation (CH or DP) is not effective, emphasizing that the timing and duration of supplementation are crucial. While chronic pre-exercise intake of collagen hydrolysate might be effective, it remains unclear if any protective effect of CH is unique or broadly applicable to protein supplementation, as increases in intramuscular collagen were unaffected by either CH or whey protein, and both provided similar results on recovery during intensified training.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The target population for this study consisted of 33 active, healthy recreationally active males aged 18 to 40 years with fair to good aerobic fitness, who were not regular protein/ergogenic supplement users, did not consume more than 1.6 g protein/kg body mass/day, and were not vegans/vegetarians. The implications are relevant for healthy individuals engaged in strenuous exercise, particularly those seeking to speed up recovery after damaging exercise.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage (EIMD) caused by strenuous exercise like downhill running results in acute muscle soreness, reduced muscle function, and transient increases in inflammatory (IL-6, hsCRP) and muscle damage (CK) markers, impacting performance and daily activities. However, the study concludes that acute, post-exercise consumption of 25g of collagen hydrolysate or dairy protein does not improve indices of EIMD during the acute recovery period in recreationally active males. Therefore, acute post-exercise protein supplementation is not considered a reliable or valuable strategy for expediting recovery from EIMD.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: While the study initially investigated interventions for protective benefit and recovery enhancement from EIMD, the primary finding indicates a lack of protective benefit from acute post-exercise collagen hydrolysate or dairy protein supplementation. EIMD itself is a normal physiological response to strenuous exercise, but the tested interventions proved an ineffective strategy for acute recovery enhancement.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study employed commonly used and validated measures for EIMD, including muscle soreness (VAS), muscle function (CMJ, IMTP, MVIC, running economy), and blood-borne biomarkers (CK, hsCRP, IL-6), which downhill running is known to specifically alter. Blood biomarkers were measured using established methods (e.g., AU5822 Clinical Chemistry Analyser, Invitrogen ELISA), with rigorous statistical analysis applied (Shapiro-Wilk, nlog transformation, Mauchley’s test, two-factor mixed ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc). However, the reliability or sensitivity of these specific biomarkers within this study was not explicitly assessed, and previous research on dairy protein's effect on EIMD markers shows mixed evidence. A significant limitation highlighted is the difficulty in accurately measuring collagen synthesis without muscle biopsies, as current biomarkers are not specific to connective tissue. The overall strategy of acute, post-exercise protein supplementation itself is deemed unreliable and not valuable for improving recovery from EIMD, attributed to issues in past protein intervention studies such as varied exercise modes, assessment criteria, dosing, timing, duration, participant history, control choice, insufficient damage levels, underpowered studies, and lack of dietary protein control.
recommended_alternatives: Standardize research methods for protein intervention studies.
Utilize more invasive measures, such as muscle biopsies, for accurate assessment of collagen synthesis.
Implement rigorous control over dietary protein intake in future studies.
Investigate different doses and combinations of proteins, as well as varied supplementation and exercise protocols.
Expand research to include diverse populations, such as females and individuals with varied fitness levels.
Consider consuming collagen hydrolysate for a prolonged period (at least nine days) prior to exercise for potential beneficial effects on recovery.
Re-evaluate acute, post-exercise protein supplementation as a strategy for expediting recovery from EIMD, as current evidence suggests it is not reliable or valuable.
